rentSupplyElasticity.source: Li (2022), "Do New Housing Units in Your Backyard Raise Your Rents?", Journal of Economic Geography: a 10% increase in housing stock within 500 ft lowers rents 1%.

alternate.source: Mense (2025), Journal of Political Economy Macroeconomics: 1% new housing supply lowers average rent 0.19%.

propertyTaxRate.source: Town of Chapel Hill FY2026-27 adopted budget: 50.0 cents per $100 of assessed value (General Fund 38.1, Debt Service 6.6, Transit 5.3), unchanged from FY2025-26. https://www.chapelhillnc.gov/files/assets/town/v/1/bmd/documents/budgets/26-27-budget-development/26-27-adopted-budget/04-projections.pdf

canopyMinPct.source: Chapel Hill Land Use Management Ordinance (LUMO) Section 5.7: tree canopy minimums of 20-40%.
canopyMinPct.note: Which value in that range applies to each zone state is our mapping, not the ordinance's. Forest counts as full canopy.

unitsPerAcre.source: Town of Chapel Hill Future Land Use Map, "Charting Our Future" (Dec 2020): Low Residential 1-4 units/acre, High Residential 8-15+, https://online.flippingbook.com/view/26191/1/ ; last codified LUMO Table 3.8-1 density caps (R-2 4.0, R-5 and R-6 15.0), https://api.municode.com/CodesContent?jobId=426902&nodeId=PTIICO_APXALAUSMA_ART3ZODIUSDIST_3.8DIST&productId=19952 ; approved mixed-use projects: Fordham Blvd Apartments (Chapelboro, 2017-05-09) https://chapelboro.com/news/development/proposal-calls-273-apartment-units-fordham-boulevard , Aura Blue Hill (News & Observer, 2021-10-28) https://www.yahoo.com/news/developer-request-leaves-chapel-hill-094500130.html , 101 E. Rosemary St (Town staff report, 2023) https://chapelhill.legistar1.com/chapelhill/attachments/9c06f852-7dd9-4b44-9094-b9564b4d7141.docx
unitsPerAcre.note: Which district stands for which zone state is our mapping. mixed_use 70 is the low end of three approved Chapel Hill projects (about 70, 99 and 214 units/acre, our calculation); a suburban-village style (MU-V arterial cap) would be about 20. Chapel Hill removed its residential density caps in 2023 (Ord. 2023-06-21/O-6).

treesPerAcre.source: USDA Forest Service FIA, EVALIDator (FIADB-API), NC 2024 evaluation, Piedmont unit 3703: 30.5 live trees per acre at 13 in. DBH or more. https://apps.fs.usda.gov/fiadb-api/fullreport?snum=4&wc=372024&rselected=Unit%20code&cselected=Diameter%20class%3A%202%20inch%20class%20to%2029&outputFormat=NJSON
treesPerAcre.note: Counts large trees only (about 13 in. DBH and up), which matches the renderer's 11 m tree spacing. At 5 in. and up the Piedmont average is 177 per acre (our calculation). Not used by the metrics yet.

commuteDistancePenalty.source: ACS 2020-2024 5-year: mean travel time = B08013 (aggregate minutes) / B08303 (workers who did not work from home), by census tract. https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT5Y2024.B08013?g=160XX00US3711800 and https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT5Y2024.B08303?g=160XX00US3711800
commuteDistancePenalty.note: Our calculation: map_edge zones, assigned to tracts by centroid and weighted by acres, average 20.1 min vs 19.5 town-wide. That is inside the tracts' margins of error, so statistically indistinguishable from 0. Used by the aggregate sim; the page's commute comes from the household model.

agentScale.source: Derived: 21,189 households (occupied homes, ACS 2020-2024 5-year, B25002) / 300 simulated households.
agentScale.note: Each simulated household stands for this many real ones, so the households and priced-out counts are in real households. It was homes per simulated household (79), which counted vacant homes as households.

agentHouseholds.note: Simulated households per zone at year 0. From the household-model prototype.

agentUnits.note: Simulated homes per zone at year 0. Homes the zone rules build are added by parcel: corridor parcels to corridor, other map_edge parcels to edge, the rest to downtown. CH-LUTI's other new homes are added by its zone: downtown and north to downtown, campus to campus, east and south (which commute over 15-501) to edge. From the household-model prototype.

agentBurdenLine.source: U.S. Census Bureau ACS 2020-2024 5-year, B25070 "Gross Rent as a Percentage of Household Income", Chapel Hill town, which reports renters paying 30% or more; HUD counts households paying more than 30% of income for housing as cost-burdened. https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT5Y2024.B25070?g=160XX00US3711800
agentBurdenLine.note: Rent share of income above which burden that builds up after arrival counts toward leaving (see agentLeaveRate). The 30% line is the standard; using it in a leaving rule is our modelling choice.

agentLeaveRate.unit: per point of burden, per year
agentLeaveRate.note: Each year a renter leaves with chance 1 - e^(-rate x points), counting only burden above 30% (agentBurdenLine) that has built up since they arrived: points above the higher of 30% and their burden on arrival. Rents follow CH-LUTI and incomes grow as CH-LUTI's do, so this is rent rising faster than income. Priced out counts year-0 households only; about 1 in 100 renters per 1% rent rise above no policy (tests/agents.test.js).

agentRenterShare.note: From the household-model prototype. Corridor (new apartments near 15-501) takes downtown's value. At year 0 these give 58.6% renters town-wide against 52.6% in the ACS (2020-2024, B25003: 11,141 of 21,189 households). Kept for now because the showcase residents (data/residents.json) are seed-7 households picked by tenure; scaling these by 0.9 matches the ACS but redraws them.

agentStudentShare.source: Our calculation from ACS 2020-2024 5-year, Chapel Hill town: 21,533 enrolled in college or graduate school (B14001) less 11,204 in group quarters, mostly residence halls (B26001), leaves about 10,300 students in households; at 2.13 people per renter household (B25010) that is about 4,800 households, or 43% of the 11,141 renter households (B25003).
agentStudentShare.note: Share of renters who are students. Rounded down to the prototype's 0.4, since some students live with non-students.

agentIncomeMedian.source: Owners: ACS 2020-2024 5-year, B25119 Median household income by tenure, Chapel Hill town: $180,885. Students and other renters: the prototype's values (40,000 and 64,000) scaled by 1.08 so that, at the ACS 2020-2024 median gross rent of $1,613 (B25064), 60.8% of renters pay 30% or more of income in rent, as in B25070. https://censusreporter.org/data/table/?table=B25119&geo_ids=16000US3711800
agentIncomeMedian.note: Median household income by type (log-normal). Over 60 runs, 60.5% of year-0 renters pay 30% or more of income in rent (ACS: 60.8%) and the median pays 34.3% (ACS B25071: 36.0%). The model's renters' median income is about $55,700 against $50,439 in the ACS: the model draws rents independently of incomes, so it can't match rent burden and income at once, and rent burden is what moves households. A wider income spread fits all three better but pushed a showcase resident (Quinn) into debt with no policy.

agentIncomeSpread.note: Log-normal spread of income by type. From the household-model prototype.

agentRemoteShare.source: ACS 2020-2024 5-year, B08301 "Means of Transportation to Work", Chapel Hill town: 8,174 of 29,039 workers worked from home. https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT5Y2024.B08301?g=160XX00US3711800
agentRemoteShare.note: A 2020-24 average that includes the 2021 peak (2019-2023: 0.271).

alternate.source: Our calculation: Orange County's 2024 1-year to 2020-24 5-year ratio (22.4% / 26.8%) applied to Chapel Hill. https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT1Y2024.B08301?g=050XX00US37135

agentDurhamShare.source: U.S. Census Bureau LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES 8), NC 2023, primary jobs (JT01): 4,225 of 20,644 Chapel Hill residents' primary jobs are in Durham city. https://lehd.ces.census.gov/data/lodes/LODES8/nc/od/nc_od_main_JT01_2023.csv.gz
agentDurhamShare.note: Our calculation, joined to the LODES block crosswalk. Durham County would be 0.25.

agentCampusWorkShare.note: Of the rest, non-students working on campus (others work downtown). From the household-model prototype.

agentZoneRent.note: Rent level by zone, before calibration to the ACS median gross rent. From the household-model prototype. Corridor takes downtown's value.

agentRentSpread.note: Each home's rent varies from min to min + range of its zone level. From the household-model prototype.

agentBaseCommuteMin.note: Local commute by zone, before calibration to the ACS mean commute. Edge households also drive 15-501; corridor households don't (no distance penalty), so corridor takes downtown's value. From the household-model prototype.

roadT0Min.note: Free-flow 15-501 travel time. From the household-model prototype.

roadCapacity.source: NCDOT "Volume Over Capacity" layer (capacity lookup by Three Oaks Engineering): US-15 route 20000015068, urban Piedmont, 2 lanes per direction with median, LOS E 37,000 vehicles/day two-way. https://services.arcgis.com/NuWFvHYDMVmmxMeM/ArcGIS/rest/services/NCDOT_Volume_Over_Capacity/FeatureServer/2
roadCapacity.note: Our calculation: converted with NCDOT's standard K = 0.09 and D = 0.6. The 15-501 segment on the map is Fordham Blvd, a signalized boulevard; NCDOT's 2021 capacity table gives about 1,955 for that facility type.

roadPeakVolume.source: NCDOT 2025 AADT, station 0680000193 "US 15 WEST OF Morgan Creek Rd": 41,500 vehicles/day, segment K = 0.08 and D = 0.591. https://services.arcgis.com/NuWFvHYDMVmmxMeM/ArcGIS/rest/services/NCDOT_2025_AADTandTrafficSegments_gdb/FeatureServer/1
roadPeakVolume.note: Our calculation: peak-hour, peak-direction demand. 15-501 starts at 98% of capacity, and its load then follows CH-LUTI's car traffic.

roadBpr.note: BPR delay curve: time = t0 x (1 + alpha x (volume/capacity)^beta). From the household-model prototype.

lutiRegionalGrowth.source: PLACEHOLDER - lo and hi need citation. mid: U.S. Census Bureau decennial census households (occupied housing units), Chapel Hill town: 20,564 in 2010 (SF1 H3) https://data.census.gov/table/DECENNIALSF12010.H3?g=160XX00US3711800 and 22,118 in 2020 (P.L. 94-171 H1) https://data.census.gov/table/DECENNIALPL2020.H1?g=160XX00US3711800
lutiRegionalGrowth.note: Growth of households looking to live in the area (location choice). mid is our calculation: compound growth 2010-2020, a historical rate, not a forecast. lo and hi are a placeholder range; the CH-LUTI model had lo 0.008, mid 0.015, hi 0.022. With homes from permit trends (lutiStartShare, Census Building Permits Survey 2015-2025), this sets the no-policy growth of homes and households for every model.

lutiAccessElasticity.note: Pull of better access to jobs in the location-choice logit. The model's note: hedonic studies put housing-price elasticities to job access around 0.1-0.3, scaled by the rent elasticity; no study cited. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiVibrancyElasticity.note: Pull of busy storefronts nearby in the location-choice logit. The model's note: amenity evidence (e.g. Glaeser, Kolko & Saiz 2001, "Consumer City") is qualitative. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiJobsHousingElasticity.note: Housing demand per extra job in Town. The model's reasoning: over half of Town jobs are held by in-commuters (LODES 54k jobs vs 30k resident workers), so demand responds well below 1:1. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiBizDemandResponse.note: How fast storefront openings and closures react to local spending (stock-and-flow adjustment speed). From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiVacancyTaxLeaseUp.note: Extra share of vacant storefronts leased per year, per 1% vacancy tax. San Francisco (2022) and Washington DC tax vacant storefronts; neither has a causal evaluation yet. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiMarginalServiceCost.note: Cost of serving a new resident, relative to the average (FY2025-26 general fund / population is about $1,540 per resident). From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiHouseholdAdjust.note: Share of the gap between desired and actual households closed each quarter (leases turn over yearly). From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiMinVacancy.note: Lowest home vacancy the market reaches. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiIncomeGrowth.source: U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts, Chapel Hill town, North Carolina (ACS 5-year estimates): median gross rent $1,172 (2014-2018) and $1,483 (2019-2023); median household income $68,640 (2014-2018) and $85,825 (2019-2023). https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/chapelhilltownnorthcarolina/
lutiIncomeGrowth.note: Nominal household income growth, for rent burden in CH-LUTI and the household model. Our calculation: over those five years rent grew 4.82%/yr and income 4.57%/yr, so incomes trailed rents by 0.25 points a year. CH-LUTI's rent path rises with rentDrift (3%/yr at its central value, Zillow ZORI), so incomes grow 3% - 0.25 points = 2.75%/yr.

lutiCpi.source: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, Survey of Professional Forecasters, Third Quarter 2026: headline CPI inflation over the next 10 years (2026-2035), 2.30% a year. https://www.philadelphiafed.org/surveys-and-data/real-time-data-research/spf-q3-2026
lutiCpi.note: Inflation applied to sales tax, service costs and programme costs, and the default for the inflation what-if (shared/luti/drivers.js). Recent: CPI-U +3.4% over the 12 months to August 2026 (BLS, released September 11, 2026).

lutiRegionShare.note: Chapel Hill's share of the regional pool of movers; sets how readily households choose other places in the location-choice logit. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiUnitSizeSf.note: Size of a typical new apartment in the development pro forma. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiSoftCost.note: Soft costs (design, fees, financing) as a share of hard cost. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiOpex.note: Operating expenses as a share of rent. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiStabilizedVacancy.note: Vacancy a developer assumes for a finished building. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiHurdle.note: Developer profit on cost needed to build. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiCalibrationGap.note: In the base year the marginal site is this far short of the hurdle (a market near equilibrium). From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiBuildQuarters.note: Time from construction start to completion. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiCostDrift.note: Construction cost inflation. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiSurfaceParkingCost.note: Cost of a surface parking space. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiLandPerUnit.note: Land cost per new home by zone. The model's note: derived from Orange County land values / typical density; no source cited. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiStructuredParking.note: 1 where new homes park in a garage, 0 where they use a surface lot. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiParkingMinimum.source: Town of Chapel Hill: on January 21, 2026 the Town Council adopted Land Use Management Ordinance amendments that eliminate mandatory parking minimums across town. https://engage.chapelhillnc.gov/re-writing-our-rules-lumo-update/news_feed/town-council-adopts-lumo-amendments
lutiParkingMinimum.note: Parking required per new home today. With none required, builders build what the market asks for (marketParkingRatio in shared/luti/params.js); the housing.parkingMinimum lever can bring a requirement back.

lutiStartShare.note: Share of the Town's construction starts (about 334 homes a year, Census Building Permits Survey 2015-2025) that land in each zone. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiProjectSize.note: Homes per building when construction starts are turned into building events for a renderer. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiProjectFloors.note: Floors per building event at today's allowed floor area. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiStorefrontVacancyElsewhere.note: Storefront vacancy outside downtown at the start (downtown's 24% is the Downtown Partnership survey in shared/luti/data.js). From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiRetailSpacesPerUnit.note: Ground-floor storefronts that come with new mixed-use apartments downtown and in the East zone (1 per 40 homes). From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiSpendingFromJobs.note: Share of storefront spending that comes from people who work in Town. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiLocalSpendShare.note: Share of a zone's storefront demand that comes from its own residents; the rest follows Town-wide spending. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiGrantSize.note: Size of one small-business support grant. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiStartupGrantSize.note: Size of one start-up grant. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiHiringJobAttrition.note: Share of the jobs a hiring subsidy created that end each year. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiAtRiskMultiple.note: Grant recipients are businesses closing at this multiple of the usual rate. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiStorefrontValue.note: Assessed value of a typical storefront bay, for the vacancy tax. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiLongVacantShare.note: Share of vacant storefronts empty long enough to owe the vacancy tax. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiInCommuterTransitShare.note: Share of in-commuters who ride transit today. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiInCommuterTransitMax.note: Upper limit on that share as bus service grows. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiRidershipFromResidents.note: Share of bus ridership that follows resident population; the rest follows jobs in Town. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiPeakVC.note: Peak volume / capacity on the main corridors, for car speeds (with roadBpr). From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiSpeedKmh.note: Speeds in Town, and to Durham and RTP for out-commuters. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiIntraZoneKm.note: Typical commute length within a zone. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiCircuity.note: Street-network distance / straight-line distance between zones. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiTerminalMin.note: Park-and-walk time at the end of a car commute: downtown and campus (UNC permits, decks) vs. elsewhere and out of Town. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiBusAccessMin.note: Walk to or from a bus stop. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiActiveModeWeight.note: Bike and walk minutes count this many times an in-vehicle minute in mode choice. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiOvtWeight.note: Waiting and walking to the bus, and parking, count this many times an in-vehicle minute. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiBikeStressMin.note: Cycling stress penalty without a protected network. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiBikeNetwork.note: bikeInfraEffect is the stress removed by referenceKm of protected lanes; a longer network scales it, up to maxEffect times. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiBikeLaneCost.note: Protected bike lane cost: capital per km, yearly debt service per dollar of capital, yearly upkeep per km. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiGravityDecay.note: Distance decay in choosing a work zone. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiAccessDecay.note: Time decay in the job-accessibility index. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiHeadwayMin.source: Our calculation from Chapel Hill Transit's GTFS feed, Fall 2026 Update (valid from October 9, 2026), via the Mobility Database (feed tld-89). https://files.mobilitydatabase.org/tld-89/latest.zip
lutiHeadwayMin.note: Typical peak minutes between buses at a stop in each zone: weekday 7-9 am departures on local routes (express, park-and-ride shuttle and school routes left out), the busier direction at each stop, averaged over the zone's stops as a frequency (harmonic mean). Stops west of the Town line (Carrboro) are left out. Zones are the nearest representative point, as in shared/luti/data.js.

lutiRegion.source: outShare: ACS 2020-2024 5-year, Chapel Hill town: 9,453 workers worked outside the town (B08008) of the 20,865 who did not work from home (29,039 workers less 8,174 at home, B08301), 45.3%. https://censusreporter.org/data/table/?table=B08008&geo_ids=16000US3711800. distanceKm and headway: PLACEHOLDER - need citation.
lutiRegion.note: Commutes out of Town (Durham, RTP, Raleigh): share of resident commuters, distance in km, minutes between regional buses. LEHD LODES 2023 puts 72% of residents' primary jobs outside town, but it files many UNC System jobs at a Raleigh headquarters (19% of residents' jobs show in Wake County), so the ACS's answer from residents is used.

lutiTransitTownShare.source: Town of Chapel Hill FY2026-27 adopted budget, Transit Fund revenue projections: the Town's transit property tax ($7,491,000) and vehicle tax ($450,000) are 34% of the three partners' contributions, with UNC ($12,624,606) and Carrboro ($2,673,487). https://www.chapelhillnc.gov/files/assets/town/v/1/bmd/documents/budgets/26-27-budget-development/26-27-adopted-budget/04-projections.pdf
lutiTransitTownShare.note: Town's share of the cost of extra Chapel Hill Transit service, assuming added service is shared as today's is.

lutiRevaluationYears.source: Orange County, 2025 Property Revaluation: the 2025 revaluation is as of January 1, 2025 and the next is January 1, 2029, on a four-year cycle. https://orangecountync.gov/revaluation
lutiRevaluationYears.note: Years Orange County revalues property; each resets the base tax rate to revenue-neutral. 2033 onward assume the four-year cycle continues, to the end of a three-decade game.

lutiResidentialShareOfBase.note: Residential share of the Town's taxable value. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiRenterTaxShare.note: Share of a property tax change that renters feel, in location choice. From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiLandCatchUpQuarters.note: Land prices close the gap to an upzoning's value by 1/this each quarter (about three years). From the CH-LUTI model.

lutiAffordableGap.note: How far below the new-build market rent a home under an affordable-housing requirement rents, as a share of that rent. Used by the housing.inclusionaryPct lever.

lutiApprovalCarryPerYear.note: Extra cost of a new home per year of longer permit approval, as a share of its cost (land and loans held longer). Used by the housing.approvalMonths lever.

lutiValueOfTimePerHour.note: What a commuter would pay to save an hour, to weigh a daily parking charge against travel time. Used by the transport.parkingPriceDelta lever.

lutiCarCo2GramsPerMile.source: U.S. EPA, Greenhouse Gas Emissions from a Typical Passenger Vehicle: about 400 grams of CO2 per mile (22.2 mpg, 8,887 g CO2 per gallon of gasoline). https://www.epa.gov/greenvehicles/greenhouse-gas-emissions-typical-passenger-vehicle
lutiCarCo2GramsPerMile.note: For the commute CO2 indicator: car-km on commutes (CH-LUTI's travel step) times this. Tailpipe CO2 only, today's fleet; electric cars would lower it.

lutiTrainingCost.source: Year Up, a sectoral job-training programme evaluated by random assignment: net cost $23,135 per participant (Fein, Dastrup and Burnett 2021), as reported in J-PAL North America, Sectoral Employment Programs evidence review (2022). https://www.povertyactionlab.org/sites/default/files/publication/Evidence-Review_Sectoral-Employment_2222022_0.pdf
lutiTrainingCost.note: Cost to the Town of putting one resident through a job-training programme, rising with inflation. Year Up is a full-time, year-long programme with stipends; shorter programmes cost less.

lutiTrainingEarningsGain.source: Katz, L., Roth, J., Hendra, R. and Schaberg, K. (2022), Why Do Sectoral Employment Programs Work? Lessons from WorkAdvance, Journal of Labor Economics 40(S1): S249-S291: substantial and persistent earnings gains of 12% to 34% following training. https://www.nber.org/papers/w28248
lutiTrainingEarningsGain.note: A trained household's income rises by this share from the year after training, while it lives here. Near the middle of the published range.

lutiOtherPropertyTaxCents.source: Orange County 2025 tax bill insert: county 68.05¢ and Chapel Hill-Carrboro City Schools district 14.79¢, on top of the Town's own rate. https://www.orangecountync.gov/DocumentCenter/View/39001/tax-bill-insert
lutiOtherPropertyTaxCents.note: The rest of a Chapel Hill homeowner's property tax bill, which the Town does not set. The combined rate today is 132.84¢ per $100, so the Town's 50.0¢ is 38% of it: a player's rate change moves about a third of the bill.

lutiWorkdaysPerYear.note: Days a year a commuter parks, for parking-charge revenue. Used by the transport.parkingPriceDelta lever.

lutiTownParkingShare.note: Share of cars bound for the downtown zone (Franklin Street and north campus) that park in Town-run decks, lots and meters; the rest use UNC or private parking the Town doesn't price. Used by the transport.parkingPriceDelta lever.
